questions.stem: Which sections of Oliver's selected poems are set for study?
options: Dream Work (1986) and American Primitive (1983)
House of Light (1990) and Twelve Moons (1979)
Dream Work (1986) and House of Light (1990)
American Primitive (1983) and Twelve Moons (1979)
questions.explanation: VCAA sets every poem in these two sections. Famous poems from other books, such as 'The Summer Day', are not set, so be careful which poems you write about.

questions.stem: Which award did American Primitive win?
options: The Nobel Prize in Literature
The T. S. Eliot Prize for Poetry
The National Book Award for Poetry
The Pulitzer Prize for Poetry
questions.explanation: American Primitive won the Pulitzer Prize in 1984. Dream Work followed in 1986, so the two set sections come from the same years of Oliver's career.

questions.stem: In 'Wild Geese', what does the speaker say the reader does not have to do?
options: Work hard, or earn your place in the world through your suffering
Pray, or ask forgiveness from the people you have hurt
Fly away, or leave the place where you were born
Be good, or walk on your knees through the desert repenting
questions.explanation: The poem opens by setting aside guilt and punishing self-sacrifice. It offers the reader permission to accept themselves, which is why it is so often read aloud.

questions.stem: What do the wild geese offer the reader in 'Wild Geese'?
options: A sense that the world still calls to you and has a place for you
A warning that winter is coming soon and the reader must get ready
A memory of the speaker's childhood on her family's farm
A symbol of the reader's sins, flying away to be forgotten
questions.explanation: As the geese head home across the sky, the world 'offers itself to your imagination'. However lonely you feel, the poem says, you belong 'in the family of things'.

questions.stem: What happens in 'The Journey'?
options: The speaker follows a flock of birds through the woods until nightfall
The speaker leaves behind voices shouting bad advice to save her own life
The speaker returns to her childhood home to forgive her family at last
The speaker travels across America by car to find a new place to live in
questions.explanation: Though the voices keep calling and the whole house trembles, the 'you' of the poem walks out into a wild night. Gradually she hears a new voice, her own.

questions.stem: 'The Journey' is written in the second person ('you'). What is the effect?
options: The poem becomes a letter to a friend who has left the speaker
The speaker's own escape becomes an experience the reader shares
The poem becomes a set of rules for how other people should behave
The reader is kept at a distance from an experience the speaker keeps private
questions.explanation: Oliver likely draws on her own escape from a painful home, but 'you' lets any reader step into the poem. It feels both private and universal.

questions.stem: What idea does 'Morning Poem' express?
options: The speaker prefers the quiet of the night to the noise of the morning
The world was perfect once but has been spoiled by people
Each morning the world is made new, and anyone can respond with joy
Mornings are hardest for people who are grieving or unwell
questions.explanation: The poem pictures dawn remaking the world each day. Even someone carrying a heavy sorrow, it suggests, can feel something inside rise up to meet the morning.

questions.stem: What does the speaker watch in 'The Turtle'?
options: A turtle sleeping through the winter under frozen mud
A turtle carried off by a hawk while crossing a road
A turtle leaving the pond to dig a nest and lay her eggs
A turtle being caught by fishermen at the edge of the sea
questions.explanation: The turtle is driven by instinct rather than thought. The poem admires a creature that does exactly what it was born to do, without human doubt.

questions.stem: Which poem in Dream Work is about a composer whose art came from a troubled mind?
options: The Sunflowers
Two Kinds of Deliverance
Robert Schumann
Stanley Kunitz
questions.explanation: Schumann was a 19th-century German composer who suffered mental illness. Oliver uses him to think about art, madness and the beauty that can come out of suffering.

questions.stem: 'Stanley Kunitz' is named after an older poet. What does Oliver compare his art to?
options: Hunting: tracking an idea until it can be caught
Building: laying bricks one by one to make a strong house
Sailing: steering a small boat through a storm
Gardening: patient, careful work that makes beauty grow
questions.explanation: Kunitz was a poet and a keen gardener. The poem shows the slow labour behind work that seems to bloom without effort.

questions.stem: What does '1945-1985: Poem for the Anniversary' set side by side?
options: Oliver's childhood in Ohio and her life on Cape Cod
The birth of a child and the death of a grandparent
A summer holiday and a long winter spent alone at home
Scenes of nature now and the memory of the Holocaust
questions.explanation: Forty years after the Second World War, the poem moves between present moments in nature and the horror of the death camps. It asks how beauty and atrocity can exist in the same world.

questions.stem: How does 'The Sunflowers', the last poem in the Dream Work section, begin?
options: With an invitation to come into the field of sunflowers
With a warning to stay out of a farmer's sunflower field
With a memory of picking sunflowers for her mother
With a description of the sunflowers dying at summer's end
questions.explanation: The poem invites the reader to walk among the flowers and listen to them. Ending the section with an invitation fits Oliver's habit of drawing readers into the natural world.

questions.stem: In 'August', what is the speaker doing?
options: Picking apples for the harvest festival in the nearby town
Watching the summer heat dry up the village pond
Swimming in the sea at the end of the holidays
Eating blackberries in the woods with animal hunger
questions.explanation: The speaker crams the berries into her mouth like a wild creature. The poem celebrates the body and blurs the line between human and animal.

questions.stem: Who was Tecumseh, the subject of a poem in American Primitive?
options: A Puritan preacher who founded one of the very first towns in Massachusetts
A Shawnee leader who resisted white settlers taking Native American lands
A Spanish explorer who first mapped the coast of Cape Cod in the 1500s
A Civil War general who fought for the Union in the Ohio countryside
questions.explanation: Tecumseh led resistance to white expansion in the early 1800s, in the region where Oliver grew up. The poem confronts the dispossession of First Peoples from the land she loves.

questions.stem: What does the speaker learn in 'In Blackwater Woods'?
options: To protect the forest from the people who want to cut it down for timber
To return each autumn to the place where she was happiest as a child
To love what is mortal, hold it close, and let it go when the time comes
To leave the woods before nightfall, when the paths become dangerous
questions.explanation: The poem moves from autumn trees and loss to three things you must be able to do. Its closing lesson accepts death as part of loving anything alive.

questions.stem: In 'University Hospital, Boston', the speaker visits someone she loves who is seriously ill. Which idea in American Primitive does this poem bring closest to home?
options: Solitude: the speaker prefers to face hardship alone
Faith: prayer can protect loved ones from serious illness
Science: modern medicine is the answer to the fear of death
Mortality: everything living, including those we love, must die
questions.explanation: Most poems in the book watch death in animals and plants. Here the cycle of life and death reaches a person the speaker loves, which tests whether acceptance is possible.

questions.stem: In 'The Fish', the speaker catches and eats her first fish. What does the poem suggest?
options: Fishing is cruel, and she feels guilty for taking the fish's life
Her father taught her to fish, and she misses all the days they spent together
The fish escapes back into the sea, showing that nature cannot be owned
Eating the fish makes it part of her, joining her to the cycle of life and death
questions.explanation: The fish's death feeds the speaker's life, and she feels it become part of her. Oliver presents eating and dying as part of one connected natural world.

questions.stem: Where did Oliver live for most of her writing life, the coast and woods of many set poems?
options: San Francisco, on the Californian coast
Nashville, in the green hills of Tennessee
Provincetown, on Cape Cod in Massachusetts
Brooklyn, in the city of New York
questions.explanation: Oliver lived in Provincetown for about forty years with her partner, the photographer Molly Malone Cook. She walked the ponds, woods and shore daily with a notebook.

questions.stem: Oliver was born in 1935 in which American state, also the setting of 'Tecumseh' and 'Rain in Ohio'?
options: Ohio
Texas
Maine
Oregon
questions.explanation: Oliver grew up in Ohio and later spoke of an unhappy childhood, from which the woods were an escape. The Ohio land and its history return in American Primitive.

questions.stem: Oliver's poetry is often linked to writers such as Thoreau and Whitman. What tradition do they share?
options: Seeing nature as a wilderness that people must tame
Finding spiritual meaning through close attention to nature
Using nature mainly as a symbol of political struggle
Describing nature scientifically, without personal feeling
questions.explanation: Like the American Romantics and Transcendentalists, Oliver treats the natural world as a teacher. Walking, watching and wondering become a kind of prayer.

questions.stem: Oliver is one of the few modern poets whose books became bestsellers. Which feature of her work best explains this?
options: Difficult language and allusions that reward readers with university study
Experimental forms that break up syntax and meaning on the page
Long rhyming narratives in the style of popular nineteenth-century ballads
Plain, clear language that speaks directly to the reader about how to live
questions.explanation: Oliver writes in simple words and often addresses 'you' directly. Her poems feel like personal advice, which helps explain why they are shared so widely.

questions.stem: Which idea runs through almost all of the set poems?
options: The natural world matters mainly as a source of symbols for the self
Paying close attention to the natural world is a way of finding meaning
Nature offers an escape from human history and suffering
Human beings are separate from, and superior to, other animals
questions.explanation: Oliver watches turtles, geese, swamps and storms with great care. Attention itself becomes a moral and spiritual act in her poems.

questions.stem: How do the set poems treat death?
options: As a punishment for people who have lived selfish lives
As a final loss that nothing in nature can redeem
As part of a natural cycle in which death feeds new life
As a terrifying end that the speaker refuses to think about
questions.explanation: In 'The Fish', 'In Blackwater Woods' and elsewhere, things die and become part of other lives. Oliver does not deny grief, but she places it within a larger pattern.

questions.stem: What links 'Wild Geese' and 'The Journey'?
options: Both warn the reader against trusting their own instincts
Both celebrate the speaker's family and childhood home
Both urge the reader to accept and save themselves despite pain
Both use the wild geese as a symbol of escape from home
questions.explanation: One poem lifts the weight of guilt and the other leaves harmful voices behind. Together they suggest that caring for your own life is necessary, not selfish.

questions.stem: How do the set poems present the relationship between humans and animals?
options: Humans have drifted apart from animals and cannot return
Humans are animals too, part of the same living world
Animals exist mainly to serve and feed human beings
Animals are symbols of human emotions rather than creatures in themselves
questions.explanation: 'Wild Geese' speaks of 'the soft animal of your body', and in 'August' the speaker eats like a wild creature. Oliver keeps reminding readers that they belong to nature.

questions.stem: Poems such as 'Tecumseh' and '1945-1985: Poem for the Anniversary' show that Oliver's nature poetry also does what?
options: Treats the past as more beautiful than the present
Confronts human history and violence alongside natural beauty
Uses history mainly to explain how the landscape was formed
Celebrates the settlers who turned wild land into farms
questions.explanation: Oliver does not treat nature as an escape from history. The land carries the memory of dispossession, and beauty sits beside atrocity.

questions.stem: Which best describes the form of most of the set poems?
options: Haiku of three lines and seventeen syllables
Free verse, often in short lines with frequent enjambment
Sonnets with a strict rhyme scheme and regular metre
Long ballads in rhyming four-line stanzas with a refrain
questions.explanation: Oliver rarely uses rhyme or fixed metre. Short lines and enjambment slow the reader down and mimic the act of noticing, one detail at a time.

questions.stem: Many poems speak directly to 'you' and use commands. What is the effect?
options: The reader feels shut out of a conversation between lovers
The poems become distant lectures on correct behaviour
The speaker seems to be talking to herself, not the reader
The reader feels personally addressed and invited to change
questions.explanation: 'You do not have to be good' and the instructions in 'In Blackwater Woods' speak to the reader like a trusted guide. The direct address makes the poems intimate.

questions.stem: Many set poems begin with a close description of something in nature, then widen out. What is this structure?
options: A shift from rhyme to blank verse in the final stanza
A move from the present tense to a list of past events
A change from the speaker's voice to an animal's voice
A turn from observation to reflection on how to live
questions.explanation: A turtle, a fish or a field of geese leads the speaker to a larger thought about life, death or belonging. Noticing comes first and meaning grows out of it.

questions.stem: Which poem begins 'You do not have to be good'?
options: Morning Poem
The Sunflowers
Wild Geese
The Journey
questions.explanation: The opening line of 'Wild Geese' is one of the most quoted in modern poetry. It sets aside guilt and perfectionism at once.

questions.stem: In 'Wild Geese', what does the phrase 'the soft animal of your body' suggest?
options: Our bodies are dangerous and must be kept under control
Our bodies and instincts are natural and deserve gentleness
Our bodies are weak and must be trained to work harder
Our bodies are separate from our minds and can be ignored
questions.explanation: Calling the body a 'soft animal' treats it with tenderness rather than shame. The speaker invites the reader to let it 'love what it loves'.

questions.stem: 'Wild Geese' ends by placing the reader 'in the family of things'. What does this mean?
options: You must find a partner and start a family of your own
You must put the needs of others before your own
However alone you feel, you belong to the natural world
Your real family will welcome you home again one day
questions.explanation: The geese, the sun and the rain all have a place, and so does the reader. The phrase answers the loneliness the poem began with.

questions.stem: In 'The Journey', what does the speaker finally become 'determined to save'?
options: 'the house where you were born'
'the voices calling in the night'
'the family that would not change'
'the only life you could save'
questions.explanation: The poem ends with a resolve to save your own life, the only one you can. It turns leaving into an act of courage rather than betrayal.

questions.stem: Which poem tells the reader that to live in this world you must be able 'to love what is mortal'?
options: The Fish
Morning Poem
Crossing the Swamp
In Blackwater Woods
questions.explanation: 'In Blackwater Woods' lists three things you must be able to do: love what is mortal, hold it, and let it go when the time comes. It is Oliver's clearest statement on loss.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Oliver's poems teach us how to live.' Discuss.
options: This essay will discuss how Mary Oliver's poems teach us all how we should live
In 'Wild Geese' the geese fly high across the sky on their way back home
Oliver presents close attention to nature as a guide to living with joy and loss
Mary Oliver was an American poet who lived in Provincetown for many years
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position and names what the paragraph will prove. The others give biography, announce the essay or describe one image.

questions.stem: A student writes: "In 'August' the speaker eats blackberries." How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List the other fruits that the speaker could have eaten instead in the woods
Describe how blackberries are usually picked and sold at markets
Explain how her animal hunger blurs the line between human and nature
Add the month, the weather and the place where the blackberries grow
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what a detail suggests. Linking the speaker's wild eating to Oliver's idea that humans are animals connects evidence to theme.
